reference.source: Clinical neuromuscular and medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: POMT2 encodes protein O-mannosyltransferase 2, the obligate partner of POMT1; only the POMT1-POMT2 heterocomplex has O-mannosyltransferase activity, so a defect in either gene produces overlapping disease.
Biallelic POMT2 variants cause a dystroglycanopathy spectrum ranging from Walker-Warburg syndrome and muscle-eye-brain-like disease to milder limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.
Severe neonatal cases present with profound hypotonia, weakness, contractures and a markedly raised creatine kinase, mirroring POMT1 disease clinically.
Cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly, cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia, hydrocephalus and eye malformations characterise the severe end of the spectrum.
Milder POMT2 limb-girdle phenotypes may present later with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and preserved or only mildly reduced cognition.
Muscle immunohistochemistry shows reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan while beta-dystroglycan and the protein core are preserved.
Because POMT1 and POMT2 are clinically indistinguishable, molecular testing (usually a gene panel) is required to assign the specific gene.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive with a meaningful recurrence risk warranting genetic counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: POMT2 encodes protein O-mannosyltransferase 2, which forms an obligate heterodimeric complex with POMT1 in the endoplasmic reticulum. Neither subunit has catalytic activity alone; together they transfer mannose from dolichol-phosphate-mannose to serine and threonine residues of alpha-dystroglycan, initiating the O-mannosyl glycan later extended into the laminin-binding matriglycan chain. Biallelic loss-of-function or hypomorphic POMT2 variants therefore abolish or reduce O-mannosylation just as POMT1 defects do. Hypoglycosylated alpha-dystroglycan cannot bind laminin and other extracellular-matrix ligands, so the sarcolemma loses its link to the basal lamina (producing muscle fibre degeneration) and the pial glia-limitans fails, allowing cortical neurones to overmigrate through breaches in the basement membrane to create cobblestone lissencephaly. Disrupted matrix signalling during ocular development yields the associated eye malformations. Residual complex activity determines where a given patient sits on the phenotypic spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies of other genetic causes
Congenital myopathies and congenital myotonic dystrophy
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI for cobblestone cortex, posterior fossa anomalies and ventricular dilatation
Muscle biopsy with alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation immunohistochemistry
Targeted POMT2 sequencing within a dystroglycanopathy gene panel
Cardiac and respiratory assessment in later-presenting limb-girdle cases
Genetic counselling and carrier testing for the family
redFlags: Progressive hydrocephalus with signs of raised intracranial pressure
Neonatal respiratory or bulbar failure with feeding difficulty
Deteriorating vision suggesting retinal detachment or glaucoma
Emerging cardiac symptoms or arrhythmia in limb-girdle presentations
reference.prognosis: Severe Walker-Warburg-type POMT2 disease is usually fatal in early childhood. Muscle-eye-brain-like and limb-girdle presentations have a more variable course, with slowly progressive weakness and, in milder cases, survival into adulthood.
pitfalls: Trying to separate POMT1 from POMT2 clinically or on imaging; only molecular testing distinguishes them.
Interpreting a normal dystroglycan core protein on immunoblot as excluding the diagnosis when the defect is glycosylation.
Missing a milder limb-girdle POMT2 phenotype by expecting only the catastrophic neonatal form.
Overlooking cardiac or respiratory surveillance in patients who survive to later childhood or adulthood.
Not arranging genetic counselling once autosomal recessive inheritance is established.
references: Standard textbooks of paediatric neurology and neuromuscular disease
management: Supportive, multidisciplinary management, as no disease-modifying therapy exists across the dystroglycanopathy spectrum
Antiseizure medication for epilepsy and ventriculoperitoneal shunting for hydrocephalus in severe presentations
Respiratory monitoring and support with gastrostomy feeding where bulbar weakness threatens safe swallowing
Ophthalmological assessment and treatment of associated eye malformations
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and orthopaedic care for contractures and progressive proximal weakness, including in milder limb-girdle presentations
Cardiac and respiratory surveillance in later-presenting limb-girdle phenotypes
Genetic counselling with carrier and prenatal testing given autosomal recessive POMT2 inheritance
